newsitem.title: EAST TIMOR: At least 17 dead in East Timor poll violence.
newsitem.headline: At least 17 dead in East Timor poll violence.

text.p: K.T. Arasu

The number of people killed in poll-related violence in East Timor rose to at least 17, but the former Portuguese colony was generally calm on Friday after separatist protests whipped up by Indonesia's general elections.
The number of civilians shot dead by separatist guerrillas in the town of Los Palos, about 200 km (124 miles) east of Dili, rose to eight, the territory's police chief, Colonel Yusuf Muharam, said.
The shooting occurred late on Wednesday, and the guerrillas took three hostages.
"Soldiers managed to free two of the hostages on Thursday but the third was shot dead by the guerrillas," Muharam said.
He said three rebels were killed on Wednesday night in an attack by about 20 dissidents on a riot police post on Dili's outskirts. Four soldiers were wounded.

"They were armed with very old M-16 rifles and were continuing to return our fire," he said. "We chased after them up the hills and on Thursday morning arrested two. A few hours later we shot dead one more and injured another."
The wounded man later died, he said.
Police and residents said the capital Dili and most other areas were relatively calm on Friday after voting on Thursday for a national parliament and regional and local assemblies.
The territory's deputy police chief, Colonel Atok Rismanto, confirmed reports by residents that dissidents had burned several polling booths on Thursday.
"They burned polling booths...we are still looking for them," he said. Rismanto said several houses had also burned, but attributed this to dry conditions and not to poll violence.
Residents said the poll burning incidents took place at Los Palos, the territory's second town of Baucau and in the townships of Ermera and Aileu.

Two civilians were shot dead in Baucau on Wednesday night by guerrillas, Colonel Muharam said. On Thursday, a soldier guarding a polling booth in Ermera district was shot dead by separatists attempting to destroy the booth.

Diplomats said separatists had wanted to demonstrate their strength in East Timor, which Indonesia occupied in 1975 and annexed the next year, and the result was the worst violence in the territory in years.
The United Nations still refuses to recognise Indonesia's sovereignty over East Timor, and Portugal said on Thursday it had protested to the world body over the elections.
The Indonesian military, which maintains a strong presence in East Timor, says about 80 poorly-armed guerrillas remain in the rugged hills. Other sources suggest there are around 200.

Election figures released late Friday afternoon showed Indonesia's ruling Golkar -- experiencing a landslide elsewhere in the country -- had taken 84.4 percent of the votes counted in the mainly-Catholic territory.
The Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), swamped elsewhere, had 13.4 percent. The Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) had just over two percent.
In the remote eastern island of Flores, meanwhile, hundreds of people protested in two villages after election officials said Golkar had won all the votes, residents said.
"In Sinar Hading village, almost 300 voters were angry when the election committee announced that Golkar got 100 percent of the vote," one resident told Reuters by telephone.
"They demanded a recount which saw Golkar only getting 292 of the 409 votes cast," he said.
In Ile Padung village, 13 people were detained but released hours later on Thursday after they protested against the result of the vote count.
